summary:
What does a country sound like?
Our platform turns Earth data into sound.
In Brazil, forests create richer, fuller tones.
In Iceland, cleaner air creates a clearer, more open sound.
Hear the differences. Understand the planet.

We created a sound-based way to explore environmental differences between countries. The platform converts seven Earth-data measurements—particulate matter, ozone, nitrogen oxides, CO2, aerosols, forest height, and nighttime lights—into a layered soundscape. This allows users to hear whether a country has hazier air, more traffic-related emissions, taller forests, or brighter city lights.
details:
Earth Information Jukebox: Code Logic and Resource Analysis

Based on the project archive earth-jukebox_6.zip, reviewed on November 15, 2026. This is a static review of the files: I read the source, data and assets, but I did not run the app, the build or the Python pipeline. Where a statement is an inference rather than something I read directly, it says so.

1. What the project does

Earth Information Jukebox is a browser app for the NASA Space Apps 2026 challenge “The Earth Information Jukebox”. A 3D globe shows countries coloured by a selected climate dataset. Clicking a country opens an information panel and plays a layered soundtrack in which each dataset controls one audio parameter. The aim is accessibility: hearing climate data, not only seeing it.

The current build uses NASA data only, taken from NASA Scientific Visualization Studio (SVS) images and their colour bars. Country outlines come from Natural Earth and are used only as map geometry.

End-to-end flow

Offline (Python): SVS image frames and colour bars are decoded into numbers per country and written to `public/data/country_telemetry.json`.

Load (browser): the app fetches that JSON and the country outline file.

State (Zustand): one store holds the countries, the selected country, the selected dataset and playback state.

Render (react-globe.gl): each country polygon is filled using the colour ramp of the selected dataset.

Sound (Tone.js): six audio tracks play through effects. Mapping functions turn a country’s values into effect settings.

2. Offline data pipeline (`scripts/buildCountryData.py`)

This script is the real data source. It uses numpy, Pillow and scipy (the `cKDTree` nearest-neighbour search).

Step 1: country masks. It reads `public/data/countries.geojson` and, for each country, draws the polygon onto a blank image at 2048×1024 (and a second set at 1080p) using Pillow. The pixel positions inside each polygon become that country’s mask. This assumes the SVS frames are flat 2:1 maps where longitude and latitude map linearly to x and y. Each country gets an identifier from its two-letter code, with manual fixes for places such as Norway, France, Kosovo and Northern Cyprus. The representative point is the outline file’s label coordinates.

Step 2: colour bar lookup tables. A `ColorbarLUT` class reads one row of pixels from the plain colour bar image for each variable, converts them from sRGB to CIELAB (a colour space where distance matches visible difference), and builds a nearest-neighbour search tree. The value range comes from the bar: PM2.5 0–60 µg/m³, O3 0–70 ppb, NOx 0–40 ppb. To decode a pixel it finds the closest bar colour; if the distance exceeds a maximum threshold the pixel is discarded as invalid. A decoded value in the top 2% of the bar is flagged as censored, meaning “at least this much”.

Step 3: air pollutants. For PM2.5 (SVS 5151), O3 (SVS 5152) and NOx (SVS 5154) it loads seven PNG frames per variable from `data-raw/geos_cf/`, spread across the model run (provenance records July 20 to August 20, 2024). For each country and frame it decodes the pixels inside the mask, then takes the median, and combines the frames.

Step 4: night light. It decodes one frame (number 1100) of SVS 5475, using the change colour bar from SVS 5276, into a signed “change score” from −100 to +100 for 2012–2023. A country needs a minimum number of valid pixels.

Step 5: aerosol. From SVS 5669 it classifies pixels into aerosol types (Sea Salt, Dust, Smoke, Sulfate) and stores the dominant type and its share of classified pixels. The numeric aerosol value stays null.

Step 6: withheld layers. Forest height (SVS 4950) and CO2 (SVS 5196) are written as null with a note explaining why. Both are rotating 3D globe renders, so per-country decoding was judged unreliable.

Output: a 446 KB JSON array of 177 countries. Each record holds the seven values plus a provenance object per dataset (source, instrument, date range, unit, censoring flag, and for aerosol the dominant type and share).

What the output contains

Dataset Countries with a value Notes

PM2.5 177 Range 1.1–46.1 µg/m³, median 13.7

O3 173 Range 9.8–60.9 ppb

NOx 177 Range 0–40 ppb, median 29.9; 7 flagged censored

Night light change 177 Only 17 distinct values; 156 of 177 are exactly −100, 0 or +100

Aerosol 0 numeric 146 countries have a dominant type

Forest height 0 Withheld

CO2 0 Withheld

3. Runtime application logic

The source is about 2,500 lines of TypeScript and React.

3.1 Data loading (`src/api/dataService.ts`)

`getEarthData()` fetches `/data/country_telemetry.json` and checks it carefully: the file must be an array, each row needs an id, coordinates and a provenance map, and numbers must be finite. Anything else is treated as null.

The nitrogen oxides value is read from either the `no2` or the `nox` field. In the JSON, `no2` is a plain copy of `nox` with no provenance of its own.

`getFallbackEarthData()` runs if the main file fails to load. It builds empty records from the country outline file, with the centre of each country’s bounding box as its point. All values are null.

There is no demo-value generator any more and no network call to any external service.

3.2 State (`src/store/useDataStore.ts`)

A Zustand store holds `telemetry`, `selectedLocation`, `selectedDataset` (default PM2.5), `isAllLayers`, `isLoading`, `error`, `isPlaying` and `dataSource` (“country” or “fallback”). Key actions: `fetchTelemetry` (tries the main file, falls back to bare outlines on error), `setSelectedDataset` (also tells the audio engine which layer to emphasise), `toggleAllLayers` (solo versus full mix) and `togglePlayback`. The store therefore couples UI state directly to the audio engine.

3.3 Dataset registry (`src/data/datasets.ts`)

One definition per dataset: label, unit, SVS source and link, minimum and maximum, a colour ramp (threshold, colour and label per step), the audio effect, track name and a function that writes the spoken description. Units: PM2.5 µg/m³, O3 ppb, NOx ppb, CO2 ppm, aerosol AOD, forest height m, night light change score. The ramps are the legend and the map colours at once.

3.4 Sound mappings (`src/audio/mappings.ts`)

These pure functions are the single source of truth for the UI, the tooltips and the audio. Each takes a value (or null) and returns the setting plus a plain-language description.

Dataset Controls Logic

PM2.5 Distortion (texture) `distortion = min(0.92, (pm/120)^1.2)`, capped at 150 µg/m³; null gives a clean sound

O3 Pitch shift in steps Low ozone raises pitch (+5 semitones below 25 ppb), mid is neutral, high lowers it (−3 at 65–85, −6 above 85)

NOx Low-pass filter cutoff ≤15 ppb: 14,000 Hz; ≤30: 5,000; ≤55: 1,500; above: 500 Hz; null: 16,000 Hz

CO2 Tempo 400–435 ppm maps to 0.85×–1.45× speed (not used in practice, see below)

Aerosol Tremolo depth and rate AOD 0–1.5 maps to depth 0–1 and 1.5–6 Hz (needs a numeric value, which is null everywhere)

Forest height Pitch in steps Seven bands from −5 to +7 semitones (needs a numeric value, which is null everywhere)

Night light Tempo −100 → 0.7×, 0 → 1.0×, +100 → 1.5×

3.5 Audio engine (`src/audio/toneEngine.ts`, about 555 lines)

Signal graph: six tracks, each a player feeding an effect, then a gain, then one master limiter set to −1 dB. PM2.5 uses `Distortion`; O3 and forest use `PitchShift`; NOx uses a low-pass `Filter`; CO2 and aerosol share one track with a `GrainPlayer` and a `Tremolo`; night light uses a second `GrainPlayer`. `GrainPlayer` changes playback speed without changing pitch, which is what the tempo mappings need.

Lifecycle: `ensureAudioNodes()` builds the graph once and checks that nodes are not disposed (this guards against React’s double mount in development). `cleanNodeReferences()` disposes everything on unmount.

Solo and mix: `applyTrackMixGains()` crossfades the track gains over 400 ms. In solo mode the selected dataset’s track is loud and the others are quiet; in all-layers mode the gains are fixed per track.

Playback: starting playback unlocks the browser audio context (browsers require a user gesture), applies the selected country’s parameters through the mapping functions, and starts the players together.

3.6 Globe and interface (`src/components/EarthJukebox.tsx`, about 870 lines)

Globe: react-globe.gl with a dark texture (`earth-dark.jpg`), a night-sky background and one polygon per country at altitude 0.005 (flat, no columns). The cap colour comes from the selected dataset’s ramp; countries with no usable value are a flat dark grey (`rgba(75, 85, 99, 0.9)`).

Interaction: hover shows a tooltip with the country name and value; click selects the country, flies the camera there and opens the information panel.

Panels: dataset dropdown, legend, an information panel listing every dataset’s value for the selected country, and a Data sources panel with SVS links, the two DOIs (10.5281/zenodo.16782803 and 10.5281/zenodo.21893141) and the Natural Earth credit.

Aerosol: shows the dominant aerosol type and its share instead of a number.

Accessibility: an `aria-live` region describes the current value and what is being heard; keyboard support covers arrow keys, Space/Enter and Escape.

4. Resource usage

4.1 NASA data resources

SVS item Content How it is used

5151 GEOS-CF surface PM2.5, flat 2:1 frames and colour bar Decoded; 7 frames; PM2.5 layer

5152 GEOS-CF near-surface ozone Decoded; 7 frames; O3 layer

5154 GEOS-CF nitrogen oxides Decoded; 7 frames; NOx layer

5475 and 5276 Black Marble night lights change 2012–2023: flat frame (5475), colour bar (5276) One frame decoded; night light layer

5669 GEOS aerosols, August 19, 2025, 20:00 UTC Aerosol type classification only

4950 GEDI forest height (RH100), 3D globe renders Listed as a layer; no values

5196 DYAMOND CO2, January–March 2020, 3D point cloud Listed as a layer; no values

5313, 5533 Night lights (EIC version), air quality composite Inventoried only; not used in the data

The PM2.5, O3 and NOx layers are model output from NASA’s GEOS-CF system that assimilates observations. They are not direct measurements, and the numbers here are estimates decoded from images.

4.2 Other data

Natural Earth 1:110m country outlines (`public/data/countries.geojson`, 839 KB): map geometry for polygons and for the decoding masks. Not NASA; it is credited in the Data sources panel.

4.3 Software libraries

Runtime: React 19, react-dom, react-globe.gl (WebGL globe built on three.js), Tone.js 15 (audio), Zustand 5 (state). Declared but unused: papaparse (I found no import of it in `src/`). Build tools: Vite 8, TypeScript ~7.0.2, Tailwind CSS 4, oxlint. Python: numpy, Pillow, scipy. `scripts/requirements-nasa.txt` still lists geopandas, netCDF4, regionmask and xarray, which the pipeline script does not appear to import, and it omits the ones it does use.

4.4 Files shipped to the browser (`public/`, about 67 MB)

File Size Purpose

country_telemetry.json 446 KB All country values and provenance

countries.geojson 839 KB Country outlines

earth-dark.jpg 95 KB Globe surface

night-sky.png 904 KB Background

6 audio tracks (.mpeg, 320 kbps stereo, 44.1 kHz) about 68 MB Soundtrack

Audio durations: O3 463 s, forest height 412 s, night light 240 s, NOx 235 s, om (PM2.5) 190 s, CO2 154 s, a total of 1,694 s (28 minutes).
